prompt: A Terraform job runs in CodeBuild. Where should the AWS provider get its credentials?
hint: The machine has an identity of its own.

choices.text: From an access key in the provider block
choices.why: A key in the block is a key in the repository, for as long as the history lasts.

choices.text: From a developer's profile copied into the build image
choices.why: That makes every build act as one person, with a credential baked into an image.

choices.text: From moto's test key
choices.why: AWS refuses that key; it only works against moto.

choices.text: From the build project's role
choices.why: Right. The provider finds the role's short-lived credentials by itself.

prompt: What does `default_tags` in the provider block do?
hint: The topic got tags nobody wrote on it.

choices.text: Tags the resources that have no tags block
choices.why: Resources with their own tags get both, merged.

choices.text: Tags every taggable resource the provider creates
choices.why: Right. Written once, applied to every resource that accepts tags.

choices.text: Adds the tags to the state file, not to AWS
choices.why: The lab read them back from the topic itself.

choices.text: Activates the tags for cost allocation in billing
choices.why: Activation is a separate step in billing, lesson 24's subject.

prompt: Put the places the AWS provider looks for credentials in the order it tries them.
trap: The machine's role first is the slip: a variable set by hand would then be ignored on an EC2 instance.

prompt: Why can the state bucket not be created by the configuration whose state it holds?

choices.text: Terraform forbids creating S3 buckets in a backend configuration
choices.why: It creates buckets freely; the order is the problem.

choices.text: It needs the bucket to exist before its very first init
choices.why: Right. Hence a small separate configuration, or a CloudFormation stack, that makes it first.

choices.text: Buckets can only be created from the console
choices.why: Any API client can create one; the lab did it with Terraform.

choices.text: The bucket would be deleted by every destroy
choices.why: prevent_destroy handles that; the real issue is the first init.

prompt: Which settings of the state bucket protect against which risk? Choose all that are correct.

choices.text: Versioning lets an earlier state be recovered
choices.why: Yes. Every write keeps the previous version.

choices.text: The public access block encrypts the state
choices.why: No. It stops a public policy or ACL; encryption is a separate setting.

choices.text: prevent_destroy refuses a plan that deletes the bucket
choices.why: Yes. Even terraform destroy in the wrong directory.

choices.text: KMS encryption adds a second permission needed to read it
choices.why: Yes. Reading needs the key as well as the bucket.

choices.text: Versioning stops two applies writing at once
choices.why: No. That is the lock's job; versioning keeps the history.

prompt: A developer can read the state bucket but has no permission on the database. Can they learn the database's password?

choices.text: Quite possibly, if the state stored it, in plain text
choices.why: Right. Read access to the state bucket is read access to whatever secrets the state holds.

choices.text: No: the state only holds resource ids
choices.why: It holds every attribute Terraform read, including secrets a resource returned.

choices.text: No: Terraform masks sensitive values in the file
choices.why: sensitive hides values in the output, not in the state file.

choices.text: By running terraform apply first
choices.why: Reading the object is enough; nothing has to run.

prompt: `terraform init` warns that `dynamodb_table` is deprecated. Does locking still work?

choices.text: No: the lock is ignored until use_lockfile is set
choices.why: The lab held a lock in the table after that warning.

choices.text: For applies, but not for plans
choices.why: Plans take the lock too, which is how the second one was refused.

choices.text: Yes; the warning says it will go
choices.why: Right. A second plan was refused by the table's lock.

choices.text: If the table is in us-east-1
choices.why: The table lives in the backend's region, here São Paulo.

prompt: What makes the DynamoDB lock a lock, rather than just a record?
hint: Read the error the second plan got.

choices.text: The item has an expiry time
choices.why: There is no expiry, which is why a lock can be left behind.

choices.text: The table allows one item at a time
choices.why: It held two items in the lab, the lock and the -md5 digest.

choices.text: A write needing the key free
choices.why: Right. ConditionalCheckFailedException is the refusal.

choices.text: Terraform reads the table every second while it runs
choices.why: It writes once, conditionally, and deletes at the end.

prompt: Why does the migration set `use_lockfile` and `dynamodb_table` together for a while, instead of switching at once?
hint: Two colleagues, two versions of the configuration.

choices.text: So both versions of the configuration exclude each other
choices.why: Right. With both, every run takes the lock the other side checks.

choices.text: Because the lock file needs the table to exist
choices.why: The lock file works alone, as the last step showed.

choices.text: To copy the lock items from the table into the bucket
choices.why: Nothing is copied; locks are short-lived and remade every run.

choices.text: Because Terraform refuses use_lockfile on a bucket that already has a state
choices.why: It accepted it on this one, which had a state.

prompt: A laptop died mid-apply and every plan is now refused with a lock. What is safe to do?
hint: Make sure the other apply is really gone.

choices.text: Run every plan and apply with -lock=false from now on
choices.why: That removes the protection for everybody, permanently.

choices.text: Ask Who, then force-unlock the ID
choices.why: Right. The refusal prints the ID, and the owner confirms nothing is running.

choices.text: Delete the state object and apply again
choices.why: That is lesson 7's accident, caused on purpose.

choices.text: Wait an hour for the lock to expire by itself
choices.why: Locks do not expire; it would wait for ever.

prompt: With `use_lockfile = true`, the lock is an object next to the state whose name ends in `.___`.
Match each piece of the backend setup to what it is for.

pairs.right: Creating the bucket before anything uses it
Clearing a lock its owner abandoned

prompt: A colleague proposes keeping the state bucket's own Terraform state in that same bucket, to have one place for everything. What goes wrong?
hint: Think of recovering after the bucket is damaged.

choices.text: Nothing: S3 is durable enough to hold its own record
choices.why: Durability does not help when the configuration managing the bucket is the thing broken.

choices.text: Terraform refuses two states in one bucket
choices.why: One bucket holds many states under different keys.

choices.text: The lock would block itself forever
choices.why: Each state has its own lock; they do not collide.

choices.text: Managing the bucket would need the bucket already working
choices.why: Right. Repairing the bucket needs a state that lives inside the thing being repaired.

prompt: A state object is written 40 times a day and versioning keeps every version for 90 days. How many versions of it does the bucket hold at the end of the 90th day?
